title: How to Build Planning Agents without losing control - Yogendra Miraje, Factset
talk_summary: The speaker distinguishes static workflow agents from agentic workflows and advocates a blueprint→planner→executor→joiner architecture to keep planning controllable. He emphasizes limiting planner tools/context, designing tools from the agent's perspective, adding recursion limits, and treating evals as first-class.

takeaways.what_they_do: Generate a natural-language blueprint for each workflow, feed it to the planner, and restrict the planner to only the tools that blueprint needs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: using blueprint you can limit what tools really goes to the uh planner

takeaways.what_they_do: Use separate blueprint, planner, executor, and joiner nodes; joiner decides replan or terminate, with a recursion limit to stop loops.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Sometimes you also set some recussion limit so that your agent just like doesn't go into loop.

takeaways.what_they_do: Design tools from the agent's point of view with purpose, when-to-use description, input/output contracts, and validation checks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need to provide it tool purpose description and input output contracts

takeaways.technique: Component and end-to-end evals by metric
takeaways.what_they_do: Maintain component and end-to-end evals; use code-based checks for tool selection, LLM judge for plan-vs-blueprint, human for formatting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: treat your evals like first class citizen

takeaways.what_they_do: Avoid agentic workflows for fixed repetitive tasks; use ETL/deterministic pipelines when outcome must be predictable or cost/latency sensitive.
takeaways.evidence_quote: In case of fixed and repetitive task just probably go for ETL pipelines.

takeaways.what_they_do: Expose enterprise microservices as MCP tools so multiple AI apps can reuse one standard tool implementation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: build the MCP tool server for your tools
